originality.note: The remaining public-source hits are chart labels and survey question wording, which are facts rather than prose, and were left as they are after review.

accuracy.method: Twenty records were drawn at random with a fixed seed: twelve statistics from the statistics file and eight insights from the multi-source and single-source insights. For each record the agent opened every cited page, both the page render and the extracted text, or the saved article for web sources, and compared every figure, label, sample size and attribution. A record matches when everything is supported as stated; minor means the substance holds but a wording, attribution or page reference needed tightening; wrong means a figure or claim was contradicted by the cited page. Every minor and wrong record was corrected in the data before this page was published, and the corrections are listed here.
accuracy.note: Three of the a16z figures in ins-083 (the 76% Google share and the exact 81% and 36% to 30% splits) were read from the article's charts when the source was first synthesised and could not be re-read now because the chart images are not kept; the surrounding prose supports the rounded versions. The next evaluation should draw a fresh sample with a new seed.

Retitled and reworded, a decade-versus-year growth distinction added, a page reference corrected, and the evidence level lowered to single-source because the posting figures come from Stanford alone.

findings: We checked twenty records and found problems in eight of them. Twelve were exactly right. Six were right in substance but loose in a detail: a figure attributed to CEOs that came from a wider executive sample, a first place that was really a tie, a named theory that only one of two cited sources actually names. Two were wrong. One gave a per-company spending figure in billions where the source says millions, a slip of three orders of magnitude. The other said demand for chat-tool skills had fallen when the source shows only their share of job postings fell while the actual counts still rose.

The pattern is worth knowing. Every number that had been read from a chart or a table was correct. The failures were in the prose the agent wrote around the numbers: units, attributions and the difference between a share falling and a count falling. That is where a reader should be most careful with any AI-written synthesis, and it is why we publish the record-level results rather than a pass rate.

All eight were corrected in the data before this page went live, and one insight was downgraded from multi-source to single-source because its central figures come from one report. One record keeps three figures that were read from charts we no longer have; we say so rather than quietly leave them.
